items.readable_text:
Content:
A graph [MATH: G] (or, more precisely, undirected graph) is a pair [MATH: (V, E)] consisting of

Content:
- a set [MATH: V] of vertices (or nodes), and
- a set [MATH: E] of edges (or arcs),

Content:
such that each edge [MATH: e \in E] is associated with an unordered pair of vertices [MATH: u, v \in V.] The edge is denoted as [MATH: u-v] or [MATH: (u,v)].

Content:
For example, we can define the graph [MATH: G_1] as

Content:
[MATH: G_{1}|= (V, E),]

Content:
where

Content:
[MATH: V|= {v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}, v_{4}}andE = {e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}, e_{5}},]

Content:
such that each edge is associated with the vertices as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: e_1] | [MATH: e_2] | [MATH: e_3] | [MATH: e_4] | [MATH: e_5] |
| [MATH: v_1 - v_2] | [MATH: v_2 - v_3] | [MATH: v_3 - v_4] | [MATH: v_1 - v_3] | [MATH: v_2 - v_4] |

Content:
Although graphs are formal mathematical entities, they can be represented graphically, just like mathematical functions are depicted as curves on the coordinate plane.

Content:
The vertices of a graph are usually shown as dots or circles on a plane, and the edges are represented by straight or curved lines connecting the corresponding vertices.
However, it's important not to confuse the graph itself with its image or graphical representation.

Content:
For example, the image of the graph [MATH: G_1] can be depicted as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/abc1837881583b16b924e75d16ba15b5]

Content:
If an edge [MATH: e] is associated with a pair of vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v,] we say that [MATH: e] is incident to [MATH: u] and [MATH: v,] and also that [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are incident to [MATH: e.] For example, in the graph [MATH: G_1,] the edge [MATH: e_1] is incident to vertices [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2,] [MATH: e_2] is incident to [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_3,] and so on.

Content:
Two vertices associated with the same edge are called adjacent. Adjacent vertices must be connected in the graphical representation of a graph. For example, in the graph [MATH: G_1,] the adjacent vertex pairs are [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2, v_1] and [MATH: v_3,] and so on.

Content:
Finally, if a vertex is not incident to any edge, it is called isolated. The graph [MATH: G_1] above has no isolated vertices, but the following graph has two: [MATH: v_3] and [MATH: v_4.]

Content:

such that each edge [MATH: e \in E] is associated with an ordered pair of vertices [MATH: u, v \in V]. In other words, in a directed graph, all edges have orientations. The edges are denoted as [MATH: u \to v] or [MATH: (u,v).]

For example, we can define the directed graph [MATH: G_2] as

such that each edge is associated with the vertices as follows:

For example, in the graph [MATH: G_2,] the vertex [MATH: v_1] is incident to the tail of [MATH: e_1,] [MATH: v_2] is incident to the head of [MATH: e_1,] and we refer to the vertices [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2] as adjacent to each other.

If an edge [MATH: e] is associated with a pair of vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v,] we say that [MATH: e] is incident on [MATH: u] and [MATH: v,] and also that [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are incident on [MATH: e.]

Finally, edges defined by the same ordered pair of vertices are called parallel (or multiple), and a loop is an edge that is incident on a single vertex.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A graph [MATH: G] (or, more precisely, undirected graph) is a pair [MATH: (V, E)] consisting of

Content:
- a set [MATH: V] of vertices (or nodes), and
- a set [MATH: E] of edges (or arcs),

Content:
such that each edge [MATH: e \in E] is associated with an unordered pair of vertices [MATH: u, v \in V.] The edge is denoted as [MATH: u-v] or [MATH: (u,v)].

Content:
For example, we can define the graph [MATH: G_1] as

Content:
[MATH: G_{1}|= (V, E),]

Content:
where

Content:
[MATH: V|= {v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}, v_{4}}andE = {e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}, e_{5}},]

Content:
such that each edge is associated with the vertices as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: e_1] | [MATH: e_2] | [MATH: e_3] | [MATH: e_4] | [MATH: e_5] |
| [MATH: v_1 - v_2] | [MATH: v_2 - v_3] | [MATH: v_3 - v_4] | [MATH: v_1 - v_3] | [MATH: v_2 - v_4] |

Content:
Although graphs are formal mathematical entities, they can be represented graphically, just like mathematical functions are depicted as curves on the coordinate plane.

Content:
The vertices of a graph are usually shown as dots or circles on a plane, and the edges are represented by straight or curved lines connecting the corresponding vertices.
However, it's important not to confuse the graph itself with its image or graphical representation.

Content:
For example, the image of the graph [MATH: G_1] can be depicted as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/abc1837881583b16b924e75d16ba15b5]

Content:
If an edge [MATH: e] is associated with a pair of vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v,] we say that [MATH: e] is incident to [MATH: u] and [MATH: v,] and also that [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are incident to [MATH: e.] For example, in the graph [MATH: G_1,] the edge [MATH: e_1] is incident to vertices [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2,] [MATH: e_2] is incident to [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_3,] and so on.

Content:
Two vertices associated with the same edge are called adjacent. Adjacent vertices must be connected in the graphical representation of a graph. For example, in the graph [MATH: G_1,] the adjacent vertex pairs are [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2, v_1] and [MATH: v_3,] and so on.

Content:
Finally, if a vertex is not incident to any edge, it is called isolated. The graph [MATH: G_1] above has no isolated vertices, but the following graph has two: [MATH: v_3] and [MATH: v_4.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5b0238ea679f5afe4de88b3233a34f71]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Directed Graphs

Content:
A directed graph [MATH: G] (or digraph) is a pair [MATH: (V, E)] consisting of

Content:
- a set [MATH: V] of vertices (or nodes), and
- a set [MATH: E] of edges (or arcs),

Content:
such that each edge [MATH: e \in E] is associated with an ordered pair of vertices [MATH: u, v \in V]. In other words, in a directed graph, all edges have orientations. The edges are denoted as [MATH: u \to v] or [MATH: (u,v).]

Content:
For example, we can define the directed graph [MATH: G_2] as

Content:
[MATH: G_{2}|= (V, E),]

Content:
where

Content:
[MATH: V|= {v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}, v_{4}}andE = {e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}, e_{5}},]

Content:
such that each edge is associated with the vertices as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: e_1] | [MATH: e_2] | [MATH: e_3] | [MATH: e_4] | [MATH: e_5] |
| [MATH: v_1 \to v_2] | [MATH: v_3 \to v_2] | [MATH: v_4 \to v_3] | [MATH: v_1 \to v_3] | [MATH: v_2 \to v_4] |

Content:
In diagrams of directed graphs, the edges are represented by straight or curved arrows connecting the corresponding vertices. For example, the image of the graph [MATH: G_2] can be as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3e0c2f7bda03bcb26319ca50aad5c467]

Content:
In directed graphs, the adjacency and incidence are defined similarly to those in undirected graphs. For example, in the graph [MATH: G_2,] the vertex [MATH: v_1] is incident to the tail of [MATH: e_1,] [MATH: v_2] is incident to the head of [MATH: e_1,] and we refer to the vertices [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2] as adjacent to each other.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Parallel Edges and Loops

Content:
In undirected graphs, edges incident to the same pair of vertices are called parallel (or multiple). In directed graphs, parallel edges also must have the same direction.

Content:
For example, in the image below, the edges [MATH: e_1, e_2,] and [MATH: e_3] of the undirected graph on the left are all parallel. However, in the directed graph on the right, only [MATH: e_1] and [MATH: e_2] are parallel because [MATH: e_3] has the opposite direction.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a6383bb17a63543ecf84c324a9691468]

Content:
A loop is an edge that is incident to a single vertex. For example, in the image below, the edges [MATH: e_1] and [MATH: e_2] form loops in both graphs.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a7a4d2997e9ed707d3781f1dc15c87d2]

---

- [MATH: e_2] and [MATH: e_1] are [MATH: \bbox[3pt,border:solid 1pt]{\phantom{\textrm{parallel}}}] edges.

Item 12 — Tutorial: Isomorphic Graphs

Content:
Graphs [MATH: G] and [MATH: H] (with no parallel edges) are isomorphic if there is a bijection [MATH: f] between the vertices of [MATH: G] and vertices of [MATH: H] such that any two vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are adjacent in [MATH: G] if and only if [MATH: f(u)] and [MATH: f(v)] are adjacent in [MATH: H.]

Content:
In other words, a graph isomorphism is a bijective mapping of vertices that preserves the adjacency (connectivity by edges). We denote isomorphic graphs as [MATH: G \cong H.]

Content:
Watch out! In directed graphs, isomorphism preserves not only connectivity but also the directions!

Content:

Hence, the graphs [MATH: G_1] and [MATH: G_2] do not represent the same graph. However, they are isomorphic because the following vertex mapping preserves their adjacency:

| [MATH: G_1] | [MATH: G_3] |

| [MATH: v_2 - v_3] | [MATH: B - A] |

| [MATH: v_3 - v_5] | [MATH: A - E] |

From the table above, we can see that the vertices [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2] are adjacent in [MATH: G_1], and their images in [MATH: G_3,] [MATH: f(v_1)=D] and [MATH: f(v_2)=B] are also adjacent, and so on. Therefore, [MATH: G_1 \cong G_3.]

Content:
In general, telling whether two graphs are isomorphic is a famously difficult problem, the graph isomorphism problem. For small graphs, we may be able to guess the mapping by inspection, but for larger graphs, we may need to check many possible bijections.
